query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The introduction of a dual-phase lamellar microstructure with a specific combination of soft fcc and hard bcc phases can improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility in eutectic high-entropy alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: Eutectic high-entropy alloys with a single-phase solid solution microstructure
generation.intervention: Introduction of a dual-phase lamellar microstructure with a specific combination of soft fcc and hard bcc phases
generation.mechanism: The dual-phase microstructure allows for the combination of high strength and high ductility through the interaction of the soft fcc and hard bcc phases, which can lead to improved strain hardening and reduced microcracking
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved strength and room-temperature tensile ductility
generation.boundary: The specific combination and volume fraction of the soft fcc and hard bcc phases, as well as the processing conditions, can affect the resulting microstructure and properties
generation.uncertainty: The optimal combination and volume fraction of the soft fcc and hard bcc phases, as well as the processing conditions, are still unknown and require further investigation

falsification_experiment.design: Tensile testing of eutectic high-entropy alloys with different microstructures (single-phase vs. dual-phase lamellar) at room temperature
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the dual-phase lamellar microstructure does not show improved strength and ductility compared to the single-phase microstructure, the hypothesis is falsified

Own digest: A Promising New Class of High-Temperature Alloys: Eutectic High-Entropy Alloys

Abstract: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) can have either high strength or high ductility, and a simultaneous achievement of both still constitutes a tough challenge. The inferior castability and compositional segregation of HEAs are also obstacles for their technological applications. To tackle these problems, here we proposed a novel strategy to design HEAs using the eutectic alloy concept, i.e. to achieve a microstructure composed of alternating soft fcc and hard bcc phases. As a manifestation of this concept, an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 (atomic portion) eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was designed. The as-cast EHEA possessed a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure, and showed an unprecedented combination of high tensile ductility and high fracture strength at room temperature.
